documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Generative AI Policy for Students (August 2023)
documents.summary: Student-facing Honor Code policy. It lists supportive uses of generative AI, then says that replacing genuine engagement, passing off AI-generated work, or using AI beyond what an instructor expressly permits is academic dishonesty. It frames the policy as educational rather than punitive.
documents.stance_why: The policy says use "in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member, will be considered a violation of the Honor Code", so AI is barred unless the instructor permits it, while it also names uses it welcomes (study guides, practice problems). That is restrict, not delegates, because it sets the default itself.

units.why: Names uses the university sees as helpful: "making study guides or practice problems" and "help with understanding difficult concepts". Several uses in one sentence, so I chose P14 (study aids) as the nearest type; P12 (tutor) also fits.
units.anchor: making study guides or practice problems
units.fit_note: Sentence also lists thinking through ideas (P15) and understanding difficult concepts (P12) together.

units.why: Says misuse "impedes the University's mission" and that using AI "as a substitute for genuine engagement" is contrary to education; the reason is that doing the work builds learning, so P41.
units.anchor: Using it as a substitute for genuine engagement, or to circumvent the necessary intellectual challenges

units.why: Asks students to "think carefully about the difference between supplementing your education and replacing it"; this tells the student to remain the thinker, so P32.
units.anchor: the difference between supplementing your education and replacing it
units.fit_note: A reflective prompt rather than an explicit rule that AI must not replace thinking.

units.why: States the purpose is "not to be overly punitive" but to ensure genuine engagement. Closest to the educative-response type P68, although it is stated as purpose, not procedure.
units.anchor: not to be overly punitive, but to ensure that you engage genuinely and deeply
units.fit_note: Gives the educational (non-punitive) aim of the policy but no actual educative response to misuse.

units.why: "you will most likely use it in your chosen field" is a career-relevance statement acknowledging AI as a professional tool, so P44.
units.anchor: you will most likely use it in your chosen field
units.fit_note: Only acknowledges likely use at work; does not say courses teach AI use.

units.why: "the University also wants to ensure that you acquire the knowledge and skills that your assignments are meant to produce": limits on AI are justified by skill-building, so P41.
units.anchor: acquire the knowledge and skills that your assignments are meant to produce

units.why: "representing work that you did not produce as your own, including work generated or materially modified by AI, constitutes academic dishonesty" classifies AI-generated work passed off as one's own as dishonesty. I chose P36 (classification as misconduct) over P19 because the sentence names the category 'academic dishonesty'.
units.anchor: including work generated or materially modified by AI, constitutes academic dishonesty

units.why: "violates an instructor's articulated policy ... will be considered a violation of the Honor Code": breaking an instructor's AI rule is classed as an Honor Code violation, so P36.
units.anchor: Use of generative AI in a way that violates an instructor’s articulated policy
units.policy: Using generative AI in a way that violates an instructor's articulated policy is a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: "using it to complete coursework in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member" is a violation: when permission is absent, use is not allowed. This is the fallback rule, P06.
units.anchor: using it to complete coursework in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member
units.policy: Using generative AI to complete coursework in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member is a violation of the Honor Code.

units.why: Directs students with questions to "the Office of Academic Standards at honor@nd.edu"; a pointer to an office, P115.
units.anchor: If you have questions about this policy, please contact the Office of Academic Standards
units.fit_note: Names the office for questions about the policy; not learning support (P72).

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Statement on Generative AI and Academic Integrity (May 2023)
documents.summary: Official May 2023 statement. It welcomes useful tools but warns against replacing coursework with AI, hands authority over appropriate use to faculty, requires instructors to communicate expectations, and routes violations to the Honor Code procedures.
documents.stance_why: The statement says "the authority to define the appropriate use, study, and deployment of these technologies rests with the faculty" and gives prohibit and encourage as examples of what instructors may choose, so the document itself sets no stance.

units.why: "we want to embrace every available tool that will aid in this educational journey" is a positive statement about tools; it names benefit, not a rule, so P87.
units.anchor: we want to embrace every available tool that will aid in this educational journey

units.why: Says AI "hold[s] promise for deploying knowledge in service to others and accelerating the discovery of new knowledge": a benefit statement, P87.
units.anchor: promise for deploying knowledge in service to others and accelerating the discovery of new knowledge

units.why: Replacing "the rigorous demands of and personal engagement with their coursework" with AI "runs counter to the educational mission": limit justified by learning, P41.
units.anchor: replace the rigorous demands of and personal engagement with their coursework
units.policy: When students use generative AI to replace the rigorous demands of and personal engagement with their coursework, it runs counter to the educational mission of the University.

units.why: "the authority to define the appropriate use, study, and deployment of these technologies rests with the faculty": faculty decide, so P04.
units.anchor: the authority to define the appropriate use, study, and deployment of these technologies

units.why: Gives the example that in an introductory writing course "an instructor may choose to prohibit or strictly manage" AI: an instructor-level choice, P04.
units.anchor: an instructor may choose to prohibit or strictly manage the use of these technologies
units.fit_note: Example of one option (prohibit or strictly manage); the ability to choose is the rule.

units.why: "in other types of courses, an instructor might encourage the use of these technologies as part of a creative process": the other option is encouragement, also P04.
units.anchor: an instructor might encourage the use of these technologies as part of a creative process
units.fit_note: Example of the encouraging option; the ability to choose is the rule.

units.why: "the instructor's responsibility is to communicate to students the expectations for their course" asks instructors to state expectations; closest is P09 though it does not say syllabus.
units.anchor: the instructor's responsibility is to communicate to students the expectations for their course
units.fit_note: Does not specify the syllabus or assignment instructions as the place.

units.why: "It is the responsibility of students to conduct themselves accordingly" makes students responsible for following the course's rules, P78.
units.anchor: It is the responsibility of students to conduct themselves accordingly
units.fit_note: Does not say students must find the rules, only conduct themselves according to the expectations instructors communicate.

units.why: Students must "never to represent work they did not produce as their own, including work generated or materially modified by AI". This bans having AI produce submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: including work generated or materially modified by AI technology

units.why: Misuse where AI is used "in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member" is not allowed by default, so this is the fallback rule, P06.
units.anchor: uses generative AI in a way not expressly permitted by the faculty member
units.fit_note: The fallback is implied by the trigger for procedures rather than stated as a rule.

units.why: "the procedures and remedies outlined in the Procedural Appendix ... will be used to resolve the matter" sends violations to the formal procedure, P81.
units.anchor: the procedures and remedies outlined in the Procedural Appendix to the Honor Code

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: Policy Update: AI Editing Tools (Fall 2024)
documents.summary: Fall 2024 update explaining that AI editing tools such as Grammarly produce AI-generated text, so an instructor's gen-AI prohibition covers them unless the instructor says otherwise. It warns about detector flags and uncited AI suggestions, and tells students to check the syllabus or ask.
documents.stance_why: The update does not set whether AI is allowed; it says "if your instructor prohibits the use of gen AI ... this prohibition includes the use of editing tools", so instructors decide and the page clarifies scope.

units.why: Defines AI editing tools: they "suggest revisions to your writing, so the suggestions they make are AI-generated text". A definition, P61.
units.anchor: so the suggestions they make are AI-generated text

units.why: "this prohibition includes the use of editing tools, unless explicitly stated otherwise": a ban on AI also bars AI proofreading tools. P21 (proofread graded work) is nearest; P18 is only about treating prose differently.
units.anchor: this prohibition includes the use of editing tools, unless explicitly stated otherwise
units.fit_note: Scope clause: editing tools are covered by an instructor's AI prohibition unless the instructor says otherwise.

units.why: States that when a detector flags a text edited with an AI tool, "This is not a false positive"; it speaks about how detector results are read, P40.
units.anchor: This is not a false positive, as the detector has correctly identified the AI-generated content
units.fit_note: Tells students detector flags on editing-tool text are correct; no rule on detector use.

units.why: Says "even a small number of suggestions from an AI editing tool" can be flagged "100% likely", a warning for students about detector behavior, P40.
units.anchor: can cause it to be flagged as 100% likely to contain AI-generated text
units.fit_note: Warns of detector sensitivity rather than stating a rule.

units.why: Using AI suggestions "without proper attribution can be considered a form of academic dishonesty": non-disclosure is the violation, P28.
units.anchor: using AI-generated suggestions without proper attribution can be considered a form of academic dishonesty

units.why: "If you aren't sure, check the syllabus or ask your instructor for clarification": ask before using, P10.
units.anchor: If you aren’t sure, check the syllabus or ask your instructor for clarification

units.why: "consider citing the use of these tools if they are allowed" recommends attribution, P24.
units.anchor: consider citing the use of these tools if they are allowed

documents.unit: Office of Academic Standards, Undergraduate Academic Code of Honor
documents.title: AI Recommendations for Instructors
documents.summary: Honor Code office guidance for instructors. It tells them to remind students of AI's limits, to be explicit about expectations and consider a syllabus and Canvas statement, offers sample statements ranging from prohibition to attribution-based permission, and urges them to learn the tools.
documents.stance_why: The page gives recommendations and four sample syllabus statements (prohibit unless permitted, permit with attribution) and asks instructors to state their own expectations, so it hands the decision to instructors rather than setting a stance.

units.why: Tells instructors to "Remind students that ChatGPT and related tools do not meet the standards normally expected of academic or professional work", then lists missing citations, non-reproducibility and "hallucinations": output reliability, P31.
units.anchor: do not meet the standards normally expected of academic or professional work
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors to tell students; lists the limits but not a duty to verify.

units.why: Names "the lack of accountability for the ethical and equitable sourcing of information" as a known issue: ethical concern, P53.
units.anchor: the lack of accountability for the ethical and equitable sourcing of information

units.why: "Learning to think and write critically ... form the hard but essential core of a liberal arts education": skills as the reason to limit reliance, P41.
units.anchor: Learning to think and write critically and to use genuine sources of truth and knowledge

units.why: "Be explicit with students about your expectations regarding the use of ChatGPT": instructors state their rules, P09.
units.anchor: Be explicit with students about your expectations regarding the use of ChatGPT
units.fit_note: Covers assignments, exams and classroom, not only the syllabus.

units.why: Asks instructors to be "clear that engaging in unauthorized use of generative AI will be considered a violation of the Honor Code": misconduct classification, P36.
units.anchor: unauthorized use of generative AI will be considered a violation of the Honor Code

units.why: Says AI editing tools such as Grammarly "violate a policy that prohibits AI use"; the rule is that proofreading tools are covered by a ban, nearest P21.
units.anchor: This includes AI editing tools (such as Grammarly)
units.fit_note: Scope clause addressed to instructors: AI editing tools count as prohibited AI.

units.why: "Consider adding a specific statement in your syllabus and on Canvas": a recommendation to put the AI statement in the syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: Consider adding a specific statement in your syllabus and on Canvas

units.why: Sample statement: students "may not use any generative AI composition or editing tools, unless it is specifically permitted for the assignment". Prohibited unless permitted: P06.
units.anchor: may not use any generative AI composition or editing tools, unless it is specifically permitted

units.why: Sample statement reminds students that they "signed the Honor Code pledge", which covers the "appropriate use of generative AI tools"; reaffirming the pledge, P111.
units.anchor: you signed the Honor Code pledge, affirming that you would not tolerate
units.fit_note: The pledge is invoked as already signed; no new signing is required.

units.why: Second sample: AI composition or editing software "may not be used for assignments in this course unless specifically stated in the assignment": fallback ban, P06.
units.anchor: may not be used for assignments in this course unless specifically stated in the assignment

units.why: "Using these tools without my permission puts your academic integrity at risk" ties unauthorized use to integrity, P36.
units.anchor: Using these tools without my permission puts your academic integrity at risk

units.why: "When this use has been permitted, the content generated or modified by AI must be properly attributed": attribution requirement, P24.
units.anchor: the content generated or modified by AI must be properly attributed

units.why: Third sample says "The use of AI tools is generally acceptable in this course": default permission, P02.
units.anchor: The use of AI tools is generally acceptable in this course

units.why: AI must be attributed "like any other source ... in a manner that can be reproduced by the reader": the rule is to attribute, P24.
units.anchor: must always be attributed in a manner that can be reproduced by the reader
units.fit_note: Also treats AI like any other source (P45), which the type does not capture.

units.why: Gives what reproducible attribution contains: "the date accessed, the web address or URL accessed, and a description of the prompt": citation details, P25.
units.anchor: the date accessed, the web address or URL accessed, and a description of the prompt

units.why: "you are responsible for assessing the quality, completeness, and accuracy of the cited information": verify AI output, P31.
units.anchor: you are responsible for assessing the quality, completeness, and accuracy of the cited information

units.why: Fourth sample: students "will be required to describe the uses and process" of AI in support of their work, a written account of use, P26.
units.anchor: you will be required to describe the uses and process

units.why: Use is allowed "where assignments specifically allow it": assignment-level permission, P04.
units.anchor: where assignments specifically allow it

units.why: "Become familiar with ChatGPT and related tools" asks instructors to learn the tools before setting policy, P63.
units.anchor: Become familiar with ChatGPT and related tools

units.why: "Engage with colleagues, students, and others in dialogue regarding the use and misuse of generative AI": faculty conversation about AI. P63 chosen over P66 because it is about colleagues and discipline, not explaining rules to students.
units.anchor: Engage with colleagues, students, and others in dialogue
units.fit_note: Includes students in the dialogue, which P63 does not capture.

units.why: The page says AI will "likely become pervasive, ubiquitous, and embedded within the common applications" used by students: a forecast about built-in AI that matches no type.
units.anchor: likely become pervasive, ubiquitous, and embedded within the common applications
units.uncovered_note: Warns that AI will be embedded in common applications and tools students use; no rule attached.

units.why: "a vital conversation to which we invite your thoughts and advice" invites feedback on standards for teaching and integrity, P54.
units.anchor: a vital conversation to which we invite your thoughts and advice

units.why: "Use ChatGPT yourself and put your assignments into the system to see how it responds": instructors test their assignments with AI, P63.
units.anchor: put your assignments into the system to see how it responds
units.fit_note: Specific practice of testing assignments in AI, which P63 (learn AI) only partly captures.

units.why: "ChatGPT does not know whether it wrote a particular piece of text": asking ChatGPT whether it wrote a text is unreliable, so detection-by-asking should not be used, P39.
units.anchor: ChatGPT does not know whether it wrote a particular piece of text
units.fit_note: Concerns asking ChatGPT itself, not commercial detectors.

documents.title: Establishing AI Policies for Your Course (Syllabus Policy Language)
documents.summary: Notre Dame Learning guide for faculty. It sets out a three-level design (university, course, assignment), a Closed/Strategic/Open framework with sample clauses and examples, and accessibility and privacy practices, and it directs instructors to the Honor Code policy.
documents.stance_why: The guide offers a "Closed/Strategic/Open" framework and says to "craft your own course-level policy, selecting one of the following approaches", so it provides tiers and leaves the choice to instructors.

units.why: "A clear AI policy in your syllabus takes away the guesswork": the reason for stating a policy in the syllabus; nearest P09, but it is a rationale.
units.anchor: A clear AI policy in your syllabus takes away the guesswork
units.fit_note: Gives the reason for a syllabus statement rather than requiring it.

units.why: "Everyone gets the same rules, the same opportunities, and a fair shot at success": fairness is the reason for clear rules, P95.
units.anchor: Everyone gets the same rules, the same opportunities, and a fair shot at success
units.fit_note: Fairness argument for clarity, not for limiting AI.

units.why: "align your course policy with University Honor Code language, then tailor at the assignment level": policies at three levels kept coherent, P109.
units.anchor: align your course policy with University Honor Code language, then tailor at the assignment level
units.fit_note: Alignment is with the university layer and assignment layer, not with colleagues.

units.why: "Link to the Honor Code and any campus AI guidance": points to other sources of rules, P115.
units.anchor: Link to the Honor Code and any campus AI guidance

units.why: Course level: "State your general stance and the rationale tied to learning outcomes in your syllabus": a syllabus statement, P09. The rationale tied to learning outcomes is part of the same instruction.
units.anchor: State your general stance and the rationale tied to learning outcomes in your syllabus
units.fit_note: Also asks for the rationale tied to learning outcomes (P83).

units.why: Assignment level: "Specify what's allowed for this task (with examples), what must be cited, and the required disclosure format": per-assignment instructions, P09.
units.anchor: Specify what’s allowed for this task (with examples), what must be cited
units.fit_note: Per-assignment specification, not syllabus.

units.why: "Notre Dame uses a Closed/Strategic/Open framework": named levels of AI use, P05.
units.anchor: Closed/Strategic/Open

units.why: Closed sample: "Generative AI tools ... may not be used for any part of this course": total ban, P01.
units.anchor: may not be used for any part of this course

units.why: Closed sample: using AI for "ideas, outlines, code, or prose is considered unauthorized assistance under the ND Honor Code": misconduct classification, P36.
units.anchor: is considered unauthorized assistance under the ND Honor Code

units.why: Closed sample: "Ask if you are unsure": ask the instructor, P10.
units.anchor: Ask if you are unsure

units.why: Closed example pairs the ban with "a brief oral check (five minutes in office hours or Zoom)" where the student explains a step: oral verification, P34.
units.anchor: a brief oral check (five minutes in office hours or Zoom)
units.fit_note: Also requires handwritten work uploaded (a format change).

units.why: Strategic sample: "You may use generative AI for brainstorming and outlining only": narrow permitted uses, P15; the word 'only' makes it restrictive.
units.anchor: You may use generative AI for brainstorming and outlining only
units.fit_note: Also outlining and the closed list 'only' (P107).

units.why: Strategic sample: "Any text included in your submission must be your original writing": submitted text is the student's own, P29.
units.anchor: Any text included in your submission must be your original writing

units.why: Strategic sample: "Directly pasted AI text is not permitted": AI may not produce submitted text, P19.
units.anchor: Directly pasted AI text is not permitted

units.why: Strategic sample: the "AI use" note must "list the tool, date, prompt(s), and how you used the output": details of the citation, P25.
units.anchor: list the tool, date, prompt(s), and how you used the output

units.why: Strategic example allows AI for opposing viewpoints and an outline in a policy brief but requires original final text with independently located sources: a prose-specific rule, P18.
units.anchor: allow students to use AI to generate opposing viewpoints and an outline
units.fit_note: Example of a Strategic assignment, tied to writing a policy brief.

units.why: Open sample: "You are encouraged to use generative AI as a collaborator for idea generation, drafting, and revision": default encouragement, P02.
units.anchor: encouraged to use generative AI as a collaborator for idea generation, drafting, and revision

units.why: Open sample: "You remain responsible for accuracy, originality, and citation": student accountability, P29.
units.anchor: You remain responsible for accuracy, originality, and citation

units.why: Open sample: the "AI use" note lists "tool, date, prompt(s), and contribution": citation details, P25.
units.anchor: Include an “AI use” note (tool, date, prompt(s), and contribution)

units.why: Open sample: "mark it as such and provide attribution" when quoting or closely paraphrasing AI output: marking AI text where it appears, nearest P27 (which is about code).
units.anchor: When quoting or closely paraphrasing AI output, mark it as such and provide attribution
units.fit_note: Applies to quoted or paraphrased text, not code.

units.why: Open example invites AI for refactoring and tests "paired with a repository log and a reflective memo": process records, P26.
units.anchor: a repository log and a reflective memo on what they accepted or rejected and why
units.fit_note: Example for a software studio; also invites AI-generated code (P16).

units.why: "Provide no-cost or institutionally supported options when feasible": equitable access, P51.
units.anchor: Provide no-cost or institutionally supported options when feasible

units.why: "Accept non-AI pathways for students who opt out": AI is optional, P51.
units.anchor: Accept non-AI pathways for students who opt out

units.why: "Avoid requiring students to upload sensitive or proprietary data to public tools" because public models may retain prompts: privacy, P50.
units.anchor: Avoid requiring students to upload sensitive or proprietary data to public tools

units.why: "Offer alternatives for students using assistive technologies; ensure captioning and screen-reader compatibility": accessibility, P97.
units.anchor: ensure captioning and screen-reader compatibility in AI-enabled workflows

units.why: "Teach verification: Fact-check AI outputs, check citations": verify AI output, P31.
units.anchor: Teach verification: Fact-check AI outputs, check citations
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors as something to teach.

units.why: "Communicate your policy clearly in your syllabus and on the first day of class": communicate expectations, P09.
units.anchor: Communicate your policy clearly in your syllabus
units.fit_note: Also first day of class.

units.why: "Seek support from ND Learning or your colleagues" when adapting or explaining a policy: faculty support, P63.
units.anchor: Seek support

units.why: Points to "dozens of crowdsourced Syllabi Policies" as ready-to-use examples: supplies sample language, P110.
units.anchor: For additional ready-to-use examples, see this list of dozens of crowdsourced

units.why: "Review the official Notre Dame University-level policy on generative AI in education": points to the Honor Code policy, P115.
units.anchor: Review the official Notre Dame University-level policy

units.why: "Specify how particular assignments relate to your course-level policy so expectations remain clear": assignment-specific clarification of rules, P04.
units.anchor: Specify how particular assignments relate to your course-level policy
units.fit_note: Calls for assignment-level detail inside a course policy.

documents.unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
documents.title: CSE Guide to the Honor Code
documents.summary: CSE department honor-code guide that treats ChatGPT-style systems like any other source. It separates resources from solutions and consulting from copying with quicksort examples, requires citation and marks for copied code, and says instructors must file a report for dishonest behavior.
documents.stance_why: The guide says "in every course, the instructor has the final say about expectations of academic honesty" and describes a common policy that "should not be assumed as default", so it gives categories and examples rather than a department stance.

units.why: "in every course, the instructor has the final say about expectations of academic honesty": the instructor decides, P04.
units.anchor: in every course, the instructor has the final say about expectations of academic honesty

units.why: Says the University policy holds that output of these systems "should be regarded as the work of another, not your own": AI as another person's work, P45.
units.anchor: should be regarded as the work of another, not your own

units.why: "instructors may have different policies for different kinds of sources": rules vary by source, P04.
units.anchor: instructors may have different policies for different kinds of sources

units.why: Defines solution and resource: "A source that partially or totally fulfills that requirement is a solution; anything else is a resource." A definition of scope, P61.
units.anchor: A source that partially or totally fulfills that requirement is a solution

units.why: Example lists asking ChatGPT "Please explain quicksort to me, without writing code." as consulting a resource, which is allowed: explaining a concept, P12.
units.anchor: Please explain quicksort to me, without writing code.

units.why: Example: asking ChatGPT how to swap two variables, reading and closing the window, is consulting a resource; this is syntax help, P13.
units.anchor: How do you swap two variables in C?
units.fit_note: Also illustrates closing the window afterward (P23); first listed instance of the question.

units.why: Example: asking ChatGPT "Please implement quicksort in C" and reading the answer is consulting a solution; the guide's common policy says consulting solutions is not allowed, so P19.
units.anchor: Please implement quicksort in C
units.fit_note: Example classed under Consulting/Solutions, not allowed under the common policy but not itself a stated rule.

units.why: Example: asking ChatGPT how to swap two variables and copying and pasting the answer is copying a resource, which the sample policy allows if cited: AI code under conditions, P16.
units.anchor: and you copy and paste the answer
units.fit_note: Allowed only with citation under the common policy; the guide says not to assume this is default.

units.why: Example: copying and pasting ChatGPT's answer to "Please implement quicksort in C" is copying a solution, not allowed in the sample policy: P19.
units.anchor: you copy and paste the answer

units.why: "A course syllabus might, for each of the four activities defined above, declare whether that activity is allowed, allowed only with proper citation, or not allowed": categories of use, P05.
units.anchor: declare whether that activity is allowed, allowed only with proper citation, or not allowed

units.why: The sample homework policy is "fairly common (but should not be assumed as default)": it names categories (consulting, copying) and says nothing is default, P05.
units.anchor: the following policy is fairly common (but should not be assumed as default)
units.fit_note: Table: resources consulting allowed, copying cited; solutions consulting and copying not allowed.

units.why: "If you quote from a source or reuse a piece of code, you should cite the source": citation of copied material, which includes AI, P24.
units.anchor: reuse a piece of code, you should cite the source

units.why: "you responsible for consulting your instructor" when unclear about acceptable consultation or citation standards: ask first, P10.
units.anchor: you responsible for consulting your instructor

units.why: Warns these systems "are particularly prone to providing more help than asked for, and can easily cross over the line from resource to solution": a tool-specific warning that matches no type.
units.anchor: can easily cross over the line from resource to solution
units.uncovered_note: Warns that AI tends to give more help than requested, so students can drift into submitting a solution.

units.why: "When in doubt about how to distinguish between resources and solutions, you should ask your instructor": ask first, P10.
units.anchor: distinguish between resources and solutions, you should ask your instructor

units.why: "if you use either the words or the ideas of someone else, you must properly cite them": citation duty applied to AI as a source, P24.
units.anchor: the words or the ideas of someone else, you must properly cite them

units.why: "Standards for citation of generative AI systems are still evolving": acknowledges change, nearest P54.
units.anchor: Standards for citation of generative AI systems are still evolving
units.fit_note: Says citation standards are evolving rather than saying this guide will be revisited.

units.why: "the citation should identify the source and indicate what part of the assignment you were working on": what a citation includes, P25.
units.anchor: the citation should identify the source and indicate what part of the assignment
units.fit_note: Requires source and assignment part, not prompt/output/date.

units.why: "Different instructors may have different guidelines for citing generative AI systems": instructor-set rules, P04.
units.anchor: Different instructors may have different guidelines for citing generative AI systems

units.why: Defines copying as electronic copying and says "Copying while paraphrasing ... is still copying": a definition setting scope, P61.
units.anchor: Copying while paraphrasing (e.g., changing variable names or replacing words with synonyms) is still copying
units.fit_note: Applies to all sources including AI.

units.why: "in code, use comments to mark off exactly which lines, functions, or files are reused" with examples citing a ChatGPT share link: mark AI-derived code in place, P27.
units.anchor: use comments to mark off exactly which lines, functions, or files are reused

units.why: "you must clearly indicate exactly what part of the assignment is copied from that source": precise marking of copied material, P27.
units.anchor: you must clearly indicate exactly what part of the assignment is copied from that source
units.fit_note: Applies to any copied source, AI included.

units.why: An instructor who sees borderline behavior "may (but is not required to) give a warning": an optional warning before escalation, nearest P68.
units.anchor: may (but is not required to) give a warning
units.fit_note: A warning for borderline behavior; not stated as educative or good-faith.

units.why: An instructor who sees dishonest behavior "is required to file" an Honor Code Violation Report or a report to the College of Engineering Honesty Committee: formal reporting, P81.
units.anchor: he or she is required to file either an Honor Code Violation Report

notes: Coder B. No school-level AI policy found. The CSE guide is a general honor-code document with AI examples; only AI-related passages coded (the pledge and non-AI collaboration rules skipped).
